analysis.one_liner: Loosens federal sugar price supports and import limits to bring sugar prices down.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan Sugar Reform Act, with 18 Senate cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Agriculture Committee and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal policy keeps U.S. sugar prices far above world levels by guaranteeing processors loans at a set price, limiting how much sugar each producer can sell, and capping sugar imports. This bill would lower the guaranteed loan rate for sugarcane to 18 cents per pound, require that supply rules be set so sugar sells at reasonable prices to consumers, raise import quotas enough to keep about a 15.5% end-of-year stockpile, and let the Agriculture Secretary suspend the program's restrictions when they hurt consumers, food workers, or small businesses. It would also repeal a program that buys surplus sugar to make ethanol.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers and food manufacturers who buy sugar: candy makers, bakers, cereal and beverage companies, and the workers at those plants, who have long paid roughly double the world price for sugar under the current program. Taxpayers also benefit when the government no longer stores or buys up excess sugar.

how_it_helps.text: The bill lowers the guaranteed loan rate for raw cane sugar to 18 cents per pound and extends beet sugar loan authority only through 2017, reducing the federal floor under sugar prices.

It requires that sugar marketing allotments be 'appropriate to maintain adequate domestic supplies at reasonable prices, taking into account all sources of domestic supply, including imports,' so supply policy must consider consumers, not just growers.

It directs the Secretary of Agriculture to set sugar import tariff-rate quotas high enough to keep end-of-year sugar stocks at roughly 15.5% of use, and lets quota shares be transferred between countries so import capacity is fully used.

It gives the Secretary authority to suspend or modify the sugar program's restrictions by weighing 'the interests of consumers, workers in the food industry, businesses (including small businesses), and agricultural producers.'
It repeals the feedstock flexibility program, which diverted surplus sugar to ethanol production, ending one more federal mechanism for absorbing excess supply instead of letting prices fall.

analysis.who_pays: Domestic sugar cane and beet growers and processors, who would face lower guaranteed prices, more import competition, and a Secretary empowered to suspend the supply and marketing rules that keep their prices high.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the current program argue world sugar prices are depressed by heavily subsidized foreign producers, so opening the U.S. market further could shift production abroad and leave the U.S. dependent on imported sugar.

Lowering the loan rate and loosening supply controls could reduce income for sugar cane and beet farmers and their rural communities, which the bill only partially cushions by keeping loans available through 2017.
The bill gives the Agriculture Secretary broad discretion to suspend or modify program provisions, which adds uncertainty about how the sugar market would actually be managed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on a small, well-organized group of growers and processors; the benefits — cheaper sugar for every food-buying household and manufacturer — are spread across the whole country. The bill retains loans and quota management rather than eliminating the program, so it is a moderate reform, not a repeal. The main honest objection is the foreign-subsidy argument, though the bill still allows the Secretary to adjust imports to prevent unreasonably high prices or avoid loan forfeitures.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee — chaired by a Democrat whose state and farm constituents include sugar interests' allies — never held a hearing or a vote, so it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen introduced the Sugar Reform Act on February 14, 2013 with nine original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Mark Kirk, Pat Toomey, Rob Portman, Bob Corker, Kelly Ayotte, and Lamar Alexander, and Democrats Dick Durbin, Frank Lautenberg, and Dianne Feinstein.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day it was introduced.
It attracted 18 total cosponsors, 12 Republicans and 6 Democrats.
The committee took no further action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar cane and beet growers and processors, who kept the price-support, supply-control, and import-quota system intact, and consumers and food manufacturers kept paying the higher sugar prices that system produces.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers kept their price supports

for.name: Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Sugar Reform Act and recruited a bipartisan group of cosponsors.

for.name: 12 Senate Republicans and 6 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support from 18 of 100 senators.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after referring it on the day of introduction, letting it expire with the Congress.

against.name: Sugar producers (cane and beet growers and processors)
against.role: Beneficiaries of the federal sugar program
against.what_they_did: Fought to preserve the sugar program's price supports, supply controls, and import quotas during the 2013 farm bill debate, and the farm bill enacted in 2014 kept the sugar program essentially intact.

sides.party_line_note: Support was genuinely bipartisan — 12 Republicans and 6 Democrats cosponsored — but the bill died in a Senate committee without ever coming to a vote, so no party-line roll call occurred.

industries.industry: Sugar cane and beet growers and processors
industries.note: The federal sugar program is this industry's economic foundation: guaranteed loans, limits on how much each producer can sell, and capped imports keep domestic sugar prices well above world levels. The bill lowers the loan floor, requires supply decisions to account for consumers, widens import quotas, and lets the Secretary suspend program rules — each directly eroding that protected revenue.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers (candy, baking, cereal, beverages)
industries.note: Sugar is a major input cost for these manufacturers, and U.S. sugar typically sells for roughly twice the world price. Cheaper, more reliably supplied sugar lowers their costs, which supports jobs in sugar-using food plants and lower retail prices.

The bill repeals the feedstock flexibility program under which surplus sugar was diverted to ethanol production. Repeal removes a federal purchase cushion that supported sugar prices, in line with the bill's goal of letting excess sugar reach the food market instead.
